miwok_falcon.name: Steal fire and bring it to the first people
miwok_falcon.notes: In the Sierra and Coast Miwok 'Theft of Fire' cycle the Prairie Falcon Wek'-wek (paired with Coyote, his grandfather) carries off fire so that humankind may have warmth and light.

sources.reference: E. W. Gifford, Miwok Myths (Univ. of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology 12, 1917), 'The Theft of Fire'

mixcoatl.name: Strike the first fire from flint and whirl the stars
mixcoatl.notes: As an avatar of Tezcatlipoca, Cloud Serpent was the first to strike fire with flint and is said to have produced the cosmic fire-drill by swirling the stars (the Milky Way) about the sky.

sources.reference: H. B. Nicholson, 'Religion in Pre-Hispanic Central Mexico,' Handbook of Middle American Indians vol. 10 (1971)

mongol_alan_gua.name: Teach the lesson of the bundle of five arrows
mongol_alan_gua.notes: Alan Gua has each of her five sons snap a single arrow with ease, then binds five arrows into one bundle that none can break, teaching that brothers divided are weak but united are invincible.

sources.reference: The Secret History of the Mongols, sect. 19-22 (trans. de Rachewiltz, 2004)

mongol_qormusta.name: Command the ninety-nine tngri of heaven
mongol_qormusta.notes: Qormusta Tngri is named chief of the ninety-nine tngri and leader of the thirty-three gods of the Mongol-Buddhist heaven, assimilated to the Indo-Iranian Indra / Ahura Mazda.

sources.reference: W. Heissig, The Religions of Mongolia (trans. 1980)

mordvin_ange_patyai.name: Maintain life and aid women in childbirth
mordvin_ange_patyai.notes: As ever-young virgin mother of the gods she is the maintainer of life in the world, protectress of girls and of morality, and the helper of married women at childbirth who guards the health of the newborn.

sources.reference: J. Abercromby, 'The Beliefs and Religious Superstitions of the Mordvins,' Folk-Lore Journal 7 (1889)

mordvin_norovava.name: Quicken and ripen the standing grain
mordvin_norovava.notes: The Grain-Mother (norov 'corn' + ava 'mother') makes the cornfields ripen; in the Erzya egg-cosmology her union with the sun-god Chipaz produces the earth-lord Mastorpaz.

sources.reference: M. Sarv, 'Mordvinian Mythology,' Folklore (Tartu) 17 (2001)

mordvin_varmanpaz.name: Raise and drive the winds
mordvin_varmanpaz.notes: Erzya male wind-god, son of the sun-god Chipaz in the egg-cosmology recorded by Sarv; he governs the moving winds, distinct from the wind-mother Varma-ava.

sources.reference: M. Sarv, 'Mordvinian Mythology,' Folklore (Tartu) 17 (2001)

mordvin_mastorpaz.name: Rule the underworld and the dead beneath the earth
mordvin_mastorpaz.notes: Son of the sun-god Chipaz and the grain-mother Norov-ava in the Erzya tradition, Mastorpaz is the lord of the world below the earth.

sources.reference: M. Sarv, 'Mordvinian Mythology,' Folklore (Tartu) 17 (2001)

muisca_chaquen.name: Grant swiftness and victory in the festival foot-races
muisca_chaquen.notes: As one of the lesser gods through whom the creator Chiminigagua was worshipped, Chaquén presides over the runners and ritual contests held on feast days and over the boundary-markers of the fields.

sources.reference: P. Simon, Noticias historiales de las conquistas de Tierra Firme (1627)
The Secret History of the Mongols, sect. 22 (trans. de Rachewiltz, 2004)

mesopotamian_utu.name: Worship at the Ebabbar temples of Sippar and Larsa
mesopotamian_utu.notes: Utu/Shamash was venerated at his great temples named E-babbar ('shining house') at Sippar in the north and Larsa in the south, his principal cult centres, with daily offerings and the king appearing before him as the divine judge and lawgiver.

sources.reference: A. R. George, House Most High: The Temples of Ancient Mesopotamia (1993)

mongol_tengri.name: Horse and sheep sacrifice on sacred heights
mongol_tengri.notes: Tengri the Eternal Blue Sky was honoured by libations of mare's milk and the sacrifice of horses and sheep offered on mountain-tops and open steppe (mountains being bridges between heaven and earth), accompanied by divination from the bones; the khan ruled by Tengri's mandate.

sources.reference: J.-P. Roux, La religion des Turcs et des Mongols (1984)

mordvin_ange_patyai.name: Biannual parish prayer-sacrifice (ozks) to the Birth-Mother and her daughters
mordvin_ange_patyai.notes: Public parish offerings (held no more than five times a year) were made to the chief divinities; twice a year honour was paid to Ange Patyai together with her four daughters, with communal prayer and sacrifice in the open.

sources.reference: J. Abercromby, 'The Beliefs and Religious Superstitions of the Mordvins,' Folk-Lore Journal 7 (1889)

mordvin_vedeava.name: River offerings to the Water-Mother
mordvin_vedeava.notes: As patroness of marriage, fertility and the rivers, Vedyava was invoked in Erzya and Moksha ritual poetry and received offerings at water sources, especially in connection with weddings and the bringing of water.

sources.reference: M. Sarv, 'Mordvinian Mythology,' Folklore (Tartu) 17 (2001)

mordvin_virava.name: Sacrifice in the sacred grove (keremet)
mordvin_virava.notes: The Forest-Mother, owner of the woods and game, was propitiated in the fenced sacred groves (keremet) where communal prayer and animal sacrifice were offered to the elemental spirits, the conifer groves being reserved for earth-bound powers.

sources.reference: U. Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric, Siberian Mythology (1927)

mossi_tenga.name: Offerings at the earth-shrine by the tengsoba
mossi_tenga.notes: The earth-priest (tengsoba / tengdana, 'earth-owner'), set apart from the political chief, has custody of the earth-shrine stones and offers sacrifice upon them to atone for bloodshed and the breaking of oaths and to secure the fertility of the soil.

sources.reference: E. P. Skinner, The Mossi of the Upper Volta (1964)

mountain_ok_afek.name: Taro and warfare rites in the Telefolip cult-house
mountain_ok_afek.notes: Afek founded the Telefolip, the great spirit-house holding the ancestral relics; the rites performed there were held to govern the fertility of taro gardens throughout the Min country and to underwrite success in warfare.

sources.reference: D. Jorgensen, 'Taro and Arrows: Order, Entropy and Religion among the Telefolmin' (PhD diss., Univ. of British Columbia, 1981)

muisca_sue.name: Dawn worship at the Sun Temple of Suamox (Sogamoso)
muisca_sue.notes: At the great round Sun Temple of Sugamuxi (Sogamoso) the zaque and his priests gathered before sunrise to pray the sun to rise in the east; at the summer solstice the nobles went in procession to make sacrifices for the harvest, and gold and emerald votive figures (tunjos) were deposited there.

sources.reference: P. Simon, Noticias historiales de las conquistas de Tierra Firme (1627)

muisca_chia.name: Worship at the Temple of the Moon at Chía
muisca_chia.notes: The moon-goddess, wife of the sun Sué, was honoured at her own temple in the town of Chía and figured in the Muisca lunar calendar that governed festivals and agriculture.

sources.reference: L. Duquesne, Disertacion sobre el calendario de los muiscas (1795); P. Simon, Noticias historiales (1627)

nabataean_al_uzza.name: Cult at the Temple of the Winged Lions, Petra
nabataean_al_uzza.notes: Al-Uzza, the Mighty, was venerated in Petra at the Temple of the Winged Lions, where a square 'eye-baetyl' (a stone with schematic eyes and nose) served as the aniconic image of the goddess; she was equated with Aphrodite Ourania and Isis.

sources.reference: P. C. Hammond, The Temple of the Winged Lions, Petra, Jordan 1973-1990 (1996)

nabataean_allat.name: Cult at the temple of Allat at Iram (Wadi Ramm)
nabataean_allat.notes: Allat, 'the Goddess,' was worshipped through aniconic baetyls; her temple at the foot of Jabal Ramm (Iram) bore the dedication to 'the great goddess who is at Iram,' and she was equated with Athena/Minerva.

sources.reference: Nabataean dedicatory inscription, temple at Iram (Jabal Ramm), 1st c. CE

attributes.name: Rays rising from the shoulders
attributes.notes: On Akkadian-period cylinder seals Utu rises between the mountains of the east with solar rays streaming from his shoulders.

sources.reference: J. Black and A. Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia (1992)

attributes.name: The toothed saw (šaššaru)
attributes.notes: He holds a serrated saw with which he cuts his path through the eastern mountains and, as judge, cuts through falsehood; it is his characteristic emblem.

sources.reference: J. Black and A. Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia (1992)

attributes.name: The winged solar disc
attributes.notes: His symbol is a four-pointed solar disc with wavy rays between the points; in the Neo-Assyrian period it is shown as a winged disc.

sources.reference: Tablet of Shamash (Sippar tablet, BM 91000)

attributes.name: Black eye-mask and red-and-white body stripes
attributes.notes: Cloud Serpent is marked by a black mask over the eyes and red-and-white 'candy-cane' stripes painted across the body, the diagnostic Mimixcoa face- and body-paint.

sources.reference: Codex Borgia; B. de Sahagun, Florentine Codex, Book 1

attributes.name: Hunter's bow, arrows and game-net
attributes.notes: He is distinguished by his hunting gear, the bow and arrows and the net or basket for carrying dead game.

sources.reference: H. B. Nicholson, 'Religion in Pre-Hispanic Central Mexico,' Handbook of Middle American Indians vol. 10 (1971)
B. de Sahagun, Florentine Codex, Book 2 (the Quecholli hunt of Mixcoatl)

attributes.name: Cut-conch wind-jewel pectoral (ehecacozcatl)
attributes.notes: Lord 9 Wind, the Mixtec Plumed Serpent, wears the wind-jewel: a conch shell cut at the cross-section worn on the chest, marking him as the wind/breath of life.

sources.reference: M. E. R. G. N. Jansen and G. A. Perez Jimenez, Encounter with the Plumed Serpent (2007)

attributes.name: Red duck-bill buccal mask
attributes.notes: He is shown wearing the buccal mask of a bird's bill over the lower face, the diagnostic wind-god attribute shared with Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl.

sources.reference: Codex Vindobonensis Mexicanus I (Yuta Tnoho)

attributes.name: Grotesque bestial visage
attributes.notes: Erlig, lord and judge of the dead, is given a monstrous form, variously a bull-head or a human body with the grotesque face of a boar, and is sometimes embodied by a totemic bear.

sources.reference: W. Heissig, The Religions of Mongolia (trans. 1980)

attributes.name: Throne flanked by lions
attributes.notes: Allat is shown enthroned between paired lions that serve as throne-guardians; the famous Lion of Allat depicts the lion (her protective power) beside a gazelle she shields from bloodshed.

sources.reference: M. Gawlikowski, 'The Lions of Allat,' in The World of the Aramaeans II (2001)
M. Gawlikowski, 'The Lions of Allat,' in The World of the Aramaeans II (2001)
J. F. Healey, The Religion of the Nabataeans: A Conspectus (2001)

attributes.name: The sacred relics of the Telefolip
attributes.notes: Afek is identified with the central cult-house she founded and the ancestral relics (including her own bones in some tellings) kept within it, the source of taro fertility.

sources.reference: D. Jorgensen, 'Taro and Arrows: Order, Entropy and Religion among the Telefolmin' (PhD diss., Univ. of British Columbia, 1981)
B. Craig and D. Hyndman (eds.), Children of Afek: Tradition and Change among the Mountain-Ok of Central New Guinea (1990)
